questions.q: What is the core job of a version control system?
options: To host a website for the project
To record every change to a set of files over time and let you recall or restore any earlier version
To automatically fix bugs in code
To compile source code into an executable
questions.explain: A VCS exists to track the full history of changes to files — who changed what, when, and why — and to let you recall or restore any point in that history.

questions.q: In a distributed version control system like Git, what does every developer's clone contain?
options: Only the current version of the files
Only a link to the central server's history
The complete project history, not just the current files
Nothing until they connect to the network
questions.explain: Distributed VCS tools like Git give every clone the full history. Committing, branching, and browsing history all work offline as a result.

questions.q: In modern source-driven Salesforce development, what is treated as the source of truth?
options: Whatever is currently live in the production org
The admin's personal notes
A Git repository holding the metadata as text files
The most recent sandbox refresh
questions.explain: Source-driven development treats the org as a deployment target, not the source of truth — the Git repository holding metadata as text is the authoritative record.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a centralized version control system rather than a distributed one?
options: Git
Mercurial
Subversion
A GitHub clone of a Git repo
questions.explain: Subversion (and the older CVS) are centralized: one server holds the authoritative history, and clients hold only the current working files, not the full history.

questions.q: A commit is best described as:
options: A saved snapshot of the repository at one point in time, with a description of what changed
A request to merge one branch into another
A conflict between two developers' changes
The server that stores a repository's remote copy
questions.explain: A commit is a snapshot of the repository's state at a moment in time, paired with a message describing the change — the basic unit that makes up a repository's history.
